Foreword
Commercial computer-controlled test instruments introduced in the 1960s used a wide variety of
non-standard, proprietary interfaces and communication protocols. In 1975, the Institute of Electrical and
Electronic Engineers approved IEEE 488-1975. IEEE 488 defined a standard electrical and mechanical
interface for connectors and cables. It also defined handshaking, addressing, and general protocol for
transmitting individual bytes of data to and from instruments and computers. This standard has been updated
and is now IEEE 488.1-1987.
Although it solved the problem of how to send bytes of data between instruments and computers, IEEE 488
did not specify the data bytes’ meanings. Instrument manufacturers freely invented new commands as they
developed new instruments. The format of data returned from instruments varied as well. By the early 1980s,
work began on additional standards to specify how to interpret data sent via IEEE 488.
In 1987, the IEEE released IEEE 488.2-1987, Codes, Formats, Protocols and Common Commands for Use
with IEEE 488.1-1987. This standard defined the roles of instruments and controllers in a measurement
system and a structured scheme for communication. In particular, IEEE 488.2 described how to send
commands to instruments and how to send responses to controllers. It defined some frequently used
“housekeeping” commands explicitly, but each instrument manufacturer was left with the task of naming any
other types of command and defining their effect. IEEE 488.2 specified how certain types of features should
be implemented if they were included in an instrument. It generally did not specify which features or
commands should be implemented for a particular instrument. Thus, it was possible that two similar
instruments could each conform to IEEE 488.2, yet they could have an entirely different command set.
Standard Commands for Programmable Instruments (SCPI) is the new instrument command language for
controlling instruments that goes beyond IEEE 488.2 to address a wide variety of instrument functions in a
standard manner. SCPI promotes consistency, from the remote programming standpoint, between instruments
of the same class and between instruments with the same functional capability. For a given measurement
function such as frequency or voltage, SCPI defines the specific command set that is available for that
function. Thus, two oscilloscopes made by different manufacturers could be used to make frequency
measurements in the same way. It is also possible for a SCPI counter to make a frequency measurement using
the same commands as an oscilloscope.
SCPI commands are easy to learn, self-explanatory and account for both novice and expert programmer’s
usage. Once familiar with the organization and structure of SCPI, considerable efficiency gains can be
achieved during control program development, independent of the control program language selected.

1     Introduction
1.1     Requirements
        This volume, “Syntax and Style,” is global in nature and shall be used with all other volumes
        of the SCPI standard.                                                                             1
1.2     Organization                                                                                      2
        The first five chapters of Syntax and Style are an introduction to the overall concept of SCPI    3
        1999. They describe an overview of the standard, reference other standards, describe SCPI
        compliance criteria, and how to interpret command tables and syntax flow diagrams. The            4
        next three chapters in this volume describe the program headers, parameters and expressions       5
        from which SCPI commands and responses are built. Following this are chapters which
        describe the status reporting model, style guidelines for creating new commands, the effect       6
        of *RST on parameter values, and facilities for managing named sets of data in an                 7
        instrument.
                                                                                                          8Bode
        This volume, Syntax and Style, is the first of the four-volume set that makes up the SCPI
        1999 Standard. The second and largest volume is the SCPI Command Reference, which                 9
        contains the actual language constructs which appear in instruments. The third volume, Data      10
        Interchange Format, defines a standard representation for data sets which may be used
        between instruments and applications, between applications, or directly between                  11
        instruments. The fourth volume, Instrument Classes, defines the SCPI commands and                12
        behavior needed to implement functionality sets associated with common classes of
        instruments. These four volumes form the complete 1999 SCPI Standard and should be used          13
        as a set.                                                                                        14Bode
        This document is intended to apply to “systems” instruments. It defines both organization        15
        and content of messages at the controller-to-instrument and instrument-to-controller
        information interchange level. This document was developed so that, an instrument                16
        designed in accordance with it, shall be able to conform to IEEE Std. 488.1-1987 Standard        17
        Digital Interface for Programmable Instrumentation, and IEEE Std. 488.2-1987 Codes,
        Formats and Common Commands For Use With IEEE Std. 488.1-1987. Conformance to                    18
        IEEE 488.1-1987 and IEEE 488.2-1987 is not required by this document, recognizing that           19
        some instruments implement physical interfaces other than the IEEE 488.1-1987. However,
        SCPI is based upon the concepts and terminology used within these standards.                     20
        This document may impact the related person-to-instrument and the instrument-to-person           21
        information interchange levels. Though the main purpose of this document is to define the        22
        interface as it relates to remote control, implementation of these codes and formats may
        affect the “front panel” of the instrument involved.                                             23
                                                                                                         24
1.3     SCPI Goals
        The goal of Standard Commands for Programmable Instruments (SCPI) is to reduce                   25
        Automatic Test Equipment (ATE) program development time. SCPI accomplishes this goal
                                                                                                         26
        by providing a consistent programming environment for instrument control and data usage.
        This consistent programming environment is achieved by the use of defined program

                                                                                   Introduction    1-1
                                             1999 SCPI Syntax & Style

                   messages, instrument responses, and data formats across all SCPI instruments, regardless of
                   manufacturer.
                   A consistent program environment uses the same commands and parameters to control
                   instruments that have the same functionality. These program commands and parameters are
     1             sent from a controller to an instrument using IEEE 488.1, VXIbus, RS-232C, etc., interfaces.
                   SCPI instruments are very flexible in accepting a range of command and parameter formats,
 2                 which makes the instrument easier to program. The instrument resonses sent back to the
 3                 controller can be either data or status information. SCPI instrument response format of a
                   particular query is well-defined and reduces the programming effort to understand
 4                 instrument data and status information. Data information can be formatted so that it is
 5                 device- and measurement-independent.
 6                 SCPI programming consistency is both vertical and horizontal. Vertical programming
                   consistency defines program messages within an instrument class. An example of vertical
 7                 consistency is using the same command for reading DC voltage from several different
 8                 multimeters. Horizontal consistency is using the same command to control similar functions
                   across instrument classes. For example, the trigger command would be the same for an
 9                 identical trigger function found among counters, oscilloscopes, function generators, etc.
10                 A key to consistent programming is the reduction of multiple ways to control similar
11                 instrument functions. The philosophy of SCPI is for the same instrument functions to be
                   controlled by the same SCPI commands. To simplify learning, SCPI uses industry-standard
12                 names and terms that are manufacturer and customer supported.
13                 SCPI provides several different levels of instrument control. Simple Measure commands
14                 provide users easy and quick control of SCPI instrumentation, while more detailed
                   commands provide traditional instrument control.
15
                   SCPI is designed to be expanded with new defined commands in the future without causing
16                 programming problems. As new instruments are introduced, the intent is to maintain
17                 program compatibility with existing SCPI instruments. SCPI ATE test programs designed to
                   run with new instruments may not be compatible with existing instruments. In other words,
18                 the test programs are upward-compatible, but not downward-compatible.
19                 To promote wide industry acceptance, SCPI is publicly available for implementation by
20                 anyone, whether or not they are a member of the SCPI Consortium.
21                 The Consortium does not release working documents or provisional documentation. Only
                   approved standards are released to the public.
22
23       1.4       SCPI Usage
                   The advantage of SCPI for the ATE system programmer is reducing the time learning how to
24                 program new SCPI instruments after programming their first SCPI instrument.
25                 Programmers who use programming languages such as BASIC, C, FORTRAN, etc., to send
26                 instrument commands to instruments will benefit from SCPI. Also, programmers who
                   implement instrument device drivers for ATE program generators and/or software
                   instrument front panels will benefit by SCPI’s advantages. SCPI defines instrument

         1-2   Introduction
                               1999 SCPI Syntax & Style

      commands, parameters, data, and status. It is not an application package, programming
      language, or software intended for instrument front panel control.
      SCPI is designed to be layered on top of the hardware-independent portion of IEEE 488.2.
      SCPI can be used with controller-to-instrument interfaces such as IEEE 488.1, VXIbus,
      RS-232C, etc.                                                                                  1
1.5   Instrument Interchangeability                                                                  2
      By providing a consistent programming environment, replacing one SCPI instrument with          3
      another SCPI instrument in an ATE system will usually require less effort than with
      non-SCPI instruments. SCPI is not a standard which completely provides for interchangeable     4
      instrumentation. SCPI helps move toward interchangeability by defining instrument              5
      commands and responses, but it does not define instrument functionality, accuracy,
      resolution, connectors, etc., which is needed to provide true instrument interchangeability    6
      without affecting the ATE system hardware and software.                                        7

3     Life Cycle
      SCPI is a “living” standard. Additional commands will always be needed to meet the needs
      of new technologies and new instruments. The SCPI Consortium meets regularly to propose
      and review extensions to the command set. New commands may be proposed by members of
      the Consortium, and by other interested parties.                                              1
      Proposals accepted by the Consortium are published and distributed to member companies        2
      and are available for immediate use. Approved proposals are reviewed annually. After the      3
      annual review, a new revision of the SCPI Standard is published, and the commands become
      a permenant part of the standard.                                                             4
      All copies of the SCPI Standard contain a version year of issue. All SCPI instruments can be  5
      queried to determine the version-year to which they conform.                                  6
3.1   Adding a Capability                                                                           7
      In general, a command proposed as an extension to SCPI will be approved if it is well         8      HP076,




      formed according to the rules set forth in “Syntax and Style”, if it conforms in style to         EdChange




      commands in the subsystem where it is placed, and if there is not already a command to        9
      control the same functionality. The Consortium rejects commands only on the basis of         10
      objective criteria.
                                                                                                   11
      SCPI is designed to grow in an upwardly compatible way. For a control program, this means
      that the aditions to SCPI will not change the meanings of existing commands, and standard    12
      programs will not need to be rewritten except to add new functionality. For an instrument,   13
      upward compatibility means that the instrument functionality will not become inaccessable
      due to additions to the language; existing instruments will not become obsolete by the       14
      extension of SCPI.                                                                           15
3.2   Obsoleting a Capability                                                                      16
      It is possible that a command may someday have to be altered or deleted in order to permit
                                                                                                   17
      important new functionality to be implemented. Such an event represents the failure of the
      extension process because it breaks upward compatibility. Proposals for changes that break   18
      upward compatibility will only be accepted if there is overwhelming evidence that the
                                                                                                   19
      benefits to users and the member companies of the Consortium outweigh the cost to existing
      users.                                                                                       20
      The following commands have been deleted from the SCPI Volume II, Command Reference          21
      as a part of the SCPI life cycle process. Reuse is discouraged. Any reinstatement is to be
                                                                                                   22
      accompanied by a careful review of compatibility issues with all previous versions of the
      SCPI standard.                                                                               23
      KEYWORD                  PARAMETER FORM                    NOTES             DELETION DATE 24
      STATus                                                                       1996
                                                                                                   25
         :QUEue                                                                    1996
            :ENABle            <event_queue_list>                                  1996            26
          [:NEXT]?                                         [query only]     1996


                                                                              Life Cycle   3-1
                                             1999 SCPI Syntax & Style

         3.3       Device Dependent Commands
                   From time to time manufacturers may elect to build instruments with capabilities that are not
                   covered by a current version of this standard. Presumably the manufacturer will submit these
                   new commands into the SCPI Life Cycle process. If the consortium adopts commands that
                   are incompatible those originally used by the manufacturer, the manufacturer is permitted to
 1                 provide his original commands in subsequent products for compatibility.

4       SCPI Compliance Criteria
        This section indicates mandatory and optional capabilities of SCPI. These capabilities are
        fully specified elsewhere, in “Syntax and Style”, “Command Reference”, “Data Interchange
        Format” and IEEE 488.2, and an instrument designer shall fully comply with the referenced
        sections. Only designs conforming to these requirements shall be able to claim conformance     1
        to the SCPI specification.                                                                     2
4.1     IEEE 488.2 Requirements                                                                        3
        All SCPI instruments shall conform to the specifications for devices in IEEE 488.2, except     4
        that section 4.1 IEEE 488.1 Requirements shall be omitted where an instrument does not
        implement an IEEE 488.1 interface.                                                             5
        Additionally, a SCPI instrument shall be able to parse <compound command program               6
        header> and <compound query program header>, to handle the tree structured commands in         7
        SCPI.
                                                                                                       8
4.1.1   IEEE Mandated Commands
        All SCPI instruments shall implement all the common commands declared mandatory by             9
        IEEE 488.2.                                                                                   10
        Mnemonic               Name                                      488.2 Section                11
        *CLS                   Clear Status Command                      10.3
        *ESE                   Standard Event Status Enable Command      10.10                        12
        *ESE?                  Standard Event Status Enable Query        10.11                        13
        *ESR?                  Standard Event Status Register Query      10.12
        *IDN?                  Identification Query                      10.14                        14
        *OPC                   Operation Complete Command                10.18                        15
        *OPC?                  Operation Complete Query                  10.19
        *RST                   Reset Command                             10.32                        16
        *SRE                   Service Request Enable Command            10.34                        17
        *SRE?                  Service Request Enable Query              10.35
        *STB?                  Read Status Byte Query                    10.36                        18
        *TST?                  Self-Test Query                           10.38                        19
        *WAI                   Wait-to-Continue Command                  10.39
                                                                                                      20
4.1.2   IEEE Optional Common Commands                                                                 21
        IEEE Std. 488.2 describes several optional commands which may be implemented in a             22
        device. None of these commands are required by SCPI.
                                                                                                      23
4.1.3   IEEE Common Command Implications                                                               KI005
        Proper implementation of some of the IEEE 488.2 common commands carry some                    24
        implications which are not immediately obvious. Primarily this has to do with the             25
        synchronization commands.
                                                                                                      26


                                                                  SCPI Compliance Criteria      4-1
                                             1999 SCPI Syntax & Style

         4.1.3.1      Overlapped and Sequential Commands
                   IEEE 488.2 defines a distinction between overlapped and sequential commands. As defined         KI005
                   in IEEE 488.2, a sequential command is one which finishes executing before the next
                   command starts executing. An overlapped command is one which does not finish executing
                   before the next command starts executing. These types of commands are described in IEEE
 1                 488.2, section 12. Examples are given in IEEE 488.2, appendix B.
 2                 IEEE 488.2 defines three common commands (*OPC, *WAI, *OPC?) which a device                     KI005
 3                 controller can use to synchronize its operation to the execution of overlapped commands.
                   The definitions for these common commands appear in sections 10.18, 10.19, and 10.39 of
     4             IEEE 488.2. All three are required by IEEE 488.2, even if none of the device’s commands
 5                 are overlapped.
 6                 Implementing any device commands as overlapped will increase the complexity of the              KI005
                   implementation of the three synchronization common commands.
 7
                   Each overlapped command has associated with it a Pending Operation flag. The device sets        KI005
 8                 this flag TRUE when it passes the corresponding command from the Execution Control
 9                 block to the Device Action block. The device sets the flag false when the device operation is
                   finished, or has been aborted.
10
                   IEEE 488.2 defines a No Operation Pending flag. This flag is FALSE whenever any Pending         KI005
11                 Operation flag is TRUE, and is TRUE whenever all Pending Operation flags are FALSE.
12                 IEEE 488.2 also permits device designers to decide which overlapped commands are
                   included in the No Operation Pending flag. A device may implement commands which
13                 select which overlapped commands are included in the No Operation Pending flag, although
14                 the SCPI standard does not include such a command.
15                 IEEE 488.2 requires user documentation to clearly indicate which commands, if any, are          KI005
                   overlapped, and which overlapped commands are included and which are excluded from the
16                 No Operation Pending flag.
17       4.1.3.2     *CLS                                                                                          KI005
18                 This command clears all status data structures in a device. For a device which minimally        KI005
                   complies with SCPI, these registers are:
19
                     SESR                                           (IEEE 488.2)                                   KI005
20                   OPERation Status Register                      (SCPI)
21                   QUEStionable Status Register                   (SCPI)
                     Error/Event Queue                              (SCPI)
22
                   Execution of *CLS shall also clear any additional status data structures implemented in the     KI005
23
                   device. The corresponding enable registers are unaffected. See the table in Command
24                 Reference, 20.7.
25                 *CLS forces the device into OCIS and OQIS (see 4.1.3.3 and 4.1.3.4) without setting the No      KI005
                   Operation Pending flag TRUE and without setting the OPC bit of the SESR TRUE and
26
                   without placing a “1” into the Output Queue.
                                                                                                                   KI005

         4-2   SCPI Compliance Criteria
                                     1999 SCPI Syntax & Style

          For example, suppose a device implements INITiate[:IMMediate] as an overlapped
          command. Assuming that the trigger model is programmed so that it will eventually return to
          the IDLE state, and that INITiate[:IMMediate] takes longer to execute than *OPC, sending
          these commands to this device:
                INITiate;*OPC                                                                                 1
                                                                                                              KI005
          results in initiating the trigger model and, after some time, setting the OPC bit in the SESR.      2
                                                                                                              KI005
          However, sending these commands:
                                                                                                               3
                INITiate;*OPC;*CLS                                                                            KI005
                                                                                                               4
          still initiates the trigger model. Since the operation is still pending when the device executes     KI005
          *CLS, the device does not set the OPC bit until it executes another *OPC command.
                                                                                                               5
4.1.3.3      *OPC and *WAI
                                                                                                               6
                                                                                                               KI005
          A device is in the Operation Complete Command Active State (OCAS) after it has executed              7
                                                                                                               KI005
          *OPC. The device returns to the Operation Complete Command Idle State (OCIS) whenever
          the No Operation Pending flag is TRUE, at the same time setting the OPC bit of the SESR
                                                                                                               8
          TRUE. See IEEE 488.2 Fig 12-4. The following events force the device into OCIS without               9
          setting the No Operation Pending flag TRUE and without setting the OPC bit of the SESR:
                                                                                                              10
                     power on                                                                                  KI005
                     receipt of the dcas message (device clear)
                                                                                                              11
                                                                                                               KI005
                     execution of *CLS                                                                        12
                                                                                                               KI005
                     execution of *RST                                                                         KI005
                                                                                                              13
          Implementation of the *OPC and *WAI commands is straightforward in devices which                     KI005
          implement only sequential commands. When executing *OPC the device simply sets the
                                                                                                              14
          OPC bit of SESR. Executing *WAI is a no-operation. The device is, in effect, always in              15
          OCIS.
                                                                                                              16
          In devices which implement overlapped commands the implementation of *OPC and *WAI                   KI005
          is a little more complicated. After executing *OPC the device must not set the OPC bit of
                                                                                                              17
          SESR until the device returns to OCIS, even though it continues to parse and execute                18
          commands. After executing *WAI the device must execute no further commands or queries
                                                                                                              19
          until the No Operation Pending flag is TRUE, or receipt of a dcas message, or a power on.
                                                                                                              20
4.1.3.4     *OPC?                                                                                              KI005
          SCPI adds the requirement that *OPC? is implemented as a sequential command.                        21
                                                                                                               KI005
          A device is in the Operation Complete Query Active State (OQAS) after it has executed               22
                                                                                                               KI005
          *OPC?. The device returns to the Operation Complete Query Idle State (OQIS) whenever
                                                                                                              23
          the No Operation Pending flag is TRUE, at the same time placing a “1" in the Output Queue.
          See IEEE 488.2 Fig 12-6. The following events force the device into OQIS without setting            24
          the No Operation Pending flag TRUE and without placing a ”1" in the Output Queue:
                                                                                                              25
                     power on                                                                                  KI005
                                                                                                              26
                     receipt of the dcas message (device clear)                                               KI005
                                                                                                              KI005

                                                                       SCPI Compliance Criteria         4-3
                                                1999 SCPI Syntax & Style

                     Implementation of the *OPC? query is straightforward in devices which implement only
                     sequential commands. When executing *OPC? the device simply places a “1" in the Output
                     Queue.
                     The implementation of overlapped commands in a device complicates the implementation of             KI005
 1                   *OPC? and places some restrictions on the implementation of the Message Exchange
                     Protocol (MEP). IEEE 488.2 dictates that devices shall send query responses in the order that
 2                   they receive the corresponding queries (IEEE 488.2 6.4.5.4). Although IEEE 488.2
 3                   recommends that *OPC? be the last query in a program message, there is nothing to prevent
                     a controller program from ignoring this suggestion. This is why *OPC? must be sequential.
     4
         4.1.3.5        *RST                                                                                             KI005
 5                   The “*RST Conditions” chapter of Volume 1 gives pretty a lucid description of the SCPI
 6                   requirements of *RST. There are, however, some implications.
 7       4.1.3.5.1      Interaction With the Synchronization Commands                                                    KI005
                     *RST stops the execution of any overlapped commands. The natural outcome of this is that            KI005
 8                   the No Operation Pending flag will go TRUE. Execution of *RST must place the device in
 9                   OCIS before setting the No Operation Pending flag TRUE, so that the effect of any pending
                     *OPC command is nullified (that is, the OPC bit of the SESR does NOT get set).
10
         4.1.3.5.2      Implications For *SAV and *RCL                                                                   KI005
11                   In devices which implement the optional *SAV and *RCL common commands, the scope of                 KI005
12                   instrument settings affected by these commands shall be the same as that affected by *RST.
                     This means that if *RST has any effect upon a command, then so must *RCL. Conversely, if
13                   the device designer wants *RCL to have an effect upon a command, then *RST must also
14                   have an effect upon that command. Inversely, and more importantly, if the device designer
                     wants a command to be EXCLUDED from the scope of *SAV and *RCL, then it must also
15                   be excluded from the scope of *RST.
16       4.1.3.5.3      *RST and *RCL as Overlapped Commands                                                             KI005
17                   While *RST stops the execution of running overlapped commands, the instrument designer              KI005
                     may find it useful to make the *RST command, itself, overlapped. For example, if resetting
18                   requires the return to an initial position of a slow-reacting, electro-mechanical device. In this
19                   case, performance may be better served with *RST overlapped as subsequent commands
                     may be parsed and executed while the resetting is completing. Even while overlapped, the
20
                     *RST command shall always complete the resetting of device state variables before
21                   subsequent commands are processed to insure the integrity of *RST exception programming.
                     For similar reasons, *RCL may be an overlapped command.
22
                     If *RST or *RCL is overlapped, its Pending-Operation flag shall be reported in the                  KI005
23
                     No-Operation-Pending flag.
24
                     If execution of *RST or *RCL causes a device operation which is equivalent to executing an          KI005
25                   overlapped command, the device shall set TRUE the Pending-Operation flag associated with
                     that command.
26


         4-4   SCPI Compliance Criteria
                                    1999 SCPI Syntax & Style

                                                                                                            KI005
4.1.3.6     *IDN?
          IEEE 488.2 is purposefully vague about the content of each of the four fields in the response     KI005
          syntax. SCPI adds no further requirement, but here are some suggestions:
                    All devices produced by a company should implement the *IDN? response                   KI005
                    consistently.
                                                                                                             1
                    Field 1, the Manufacturer field, should be identical for all devices produced by a       2
                                                                                                             KI005
                    single company.
                    Field 2, the Model field, should NOT contain the word “MODEL”.
                                                                                                             3
                                                                                                             KI005
                    Field 4, the Firmware level field, should contain information about all separately       4
                                                                                                             KI005
                    revisable subsystems. This information can be contained in single or multiple
                    revision codes.

          describes the concepts behind SCPI and sets guidelines for originating new commands. A             9

         4.2.2      Optional Commands
                    All other commands in the “Command Reference” are considered optional, depending on the
                    capabilities of the instrument. That is, the control of any instrument capability that is
                    described in SCPI shall be implemented exactly as specified by using the appropriate SCPI
 1                  defined commands. For example, an instrument dedicated to voltage measurement would
                    not implement commands for sensing frequency. Certain commands, if implemented,
 2                  require that other commands also be implemented.
 3                  When a device does not support all alternative parameter values that are allowed for a SCPI
     4              command, it may implement a subset of these values unless otherwise stated. For example,
                    if an instrument implements only RECTangular and UNIForm data shaping for its
 5                  CALCulate:TRANSform:WINDow command, it may generate an error on receipt of any
 6                  other SCPI defined parameter value (FLATtop,HAMMing, etc). However, a device must
                    implement all parameters of a multi-parameter SCPI command.
 7
                    Commands required to implement a SCPI-described capability may be omitted under special
 8                  conditions. The special condition exists when a command to be implemented affects a part
 9                  of the instrument in which the configuration is fixed, and that the fixed configuration for that
                    command corresponds to the value it would take on when an IEEE 488.2 *RST reset
10                  command is issued. For example, an instrument with a display that is configured to be
11                  permanently on does not need to implement the command that turns the display ON or OFF,
                    since at *RST it is required by SCPI to be ON. If an instrument has a fixed configuration in
12                  which a setting does not correspond to the *RST value, then the instrument shall implement
13                  the command for that setting even though it has only a single legal value.
14       4.2.3      Documentation Requirements
                    The documentation for a SCPI instrument shall list the version number for which the
15                  instrument complies. This information shall appear on instrument specification sheets and
16                  related documents, as well as the programming manual.
17                  The manual for a SCPI instrument shall have a separate section titled “SCPI Conformance                 HP076




                    Information”. This section shall list separately:
18
                               The SCPI version to which the instrument complies
19
                               The syntax of all SCPI confirmed commands implemented by the instrument.
20                             Confirmed commands are those commands which are published in the latest
21                             version of SCPI to which the instrument conforms. Commands in the
                               DIAGnostic subsystem, and other commands which are not intended for end-user
22                             use need not be documented in this section.
23
                                                                                                                       HP000,HP001




                               The syntax of all SCPI approved commands implemented by the instrument.
24                             Approved commands are those commands which have been approved by the
25                             SCPI Consortium, but are not contained in the version of SCPI to which the
                               instrument conforms.
26                                                                                                                          HP000




                               The syntax of all commands implemented by the instrument, which are not part of

the SCPI definition.

5     Notation
        Extensive use is made of syntax flow diagrams and tables throughout this document.
        Associated with these are notational styles, which are described in this chapter.

5.1     Interpreting Command Tables                                                                          1
        Command tables are used to define a set of SCPI commands. A table shows the commands,                2
        their hierarchical relationships, related parameters (if any), and associated notes. The table is
        broken into 3 columns; the KEYWORD, the PARAMETER FORM, and any NOTES.                               3
        The KEYWORD column provides the name of the command. The actual name of the                          4
        command consists of one or more keywords since SCPI commands are based on a                          5
        hierarchical structure, also known as a tree system. In such a system, associated commands
        are grouped together under a common node in the hierarchy, analogous to the way leaves at            6
        a same level are connected at a common branch. This and similar branches are connected to
                                                                                                             7
        fewer and thicker branches, until they meet at the root of the tree. The closer to the root, the
        higher a node is considered in the hierarchy. To obtain a particular leaf or a particular            8
        command, the full path to it must be specified. This path is represented in the tables by
                                                                                                             9
        placing the highest node in the hierarchy in the left-most position. Lower nodes in the
        hierarchy are indented one position to the right, below the parent node.                            10
        Square brackets ([]) are used to enclose a keyword that is optional when programming the            11
        command; that is, the instrument shall process the command to have the same effect whether
                                                                                                            12
        the option node is omitted by the programmer or not. Such a node is called a default node.
        Letter case in tables is used to differentiate between the accepted short form (the uppercase       13
        characters) and the long form (the whole keyword). The significance of the short and long
                                                                                                            14
        form keywords is explained in the “Program Headers” chapter.
                                                                                                            15
        The PARAMETER FORM column indicates the number and order of parameters in a
        command and their legal values. A command may allow the use of a SCPI-defined                       16
        parameter type, a literal, or a combination of the two. The SCPI-defined parameter types are        17
        described in the “Parameters” chapter, and are distinguished by enclosing the type name in
        angle brackets (<>). A literal is typically a word that enumerates a setting that cannot be         18
        described using the SCPI-defined parameter types.                                                   19
        In the PARAMETER FORM column, a number of characters have special significance.                     20
        Square brackets ([]) are used to enclose one or more parameters that are optional when
        controlling the instrument. Braces ({}), or curly brackets, are used to enclose one or more         21
        parameters that may be included zero or more times. The vertical bar (|) can be read as “or”        22
        and is used to separate alternative parameter options.
                                                                                                            23
        The query form of a command is generated by appending a question mark to the last
        keyword. However, not all commands have a query form, and some commands exist only in               24
        the query form. The NOTES column is used to indicate this.                                          25
        As an example, suppose the existance of the following table.                                        26


                                                                                         Notation    5-1
                                              1999 SCPI Syntax & Style

                   KEYWORD                 PARAMETER FORM                                 COMMENTS
                   :FREQuency
                     [:CW]                 <numeric_value>
                        :AUTO              <Boolean>
                      :CENTer              <numeric_value>
 1                    :SPAN                <numeric_value>
 2
                   To set the frequency value for a Continuous Wave signal, the following command would be
 3                 sent:
 4                    FREQuency:CW 2000000
     5             Alternatively, since the CW node is optional the following command is also valid:
                      FREQuency 2000000
 6
                   To set the value of AUTO, either of the following commands are allowed, again due to the
 7                 optional CW node:
 8                     FREQuency:CW:AUTO OFF
 9                    FREQuency:AUTO           OFF
10                 The query form of the AUTO command is either of the following:
                      FREQuency:CW:AUTO?
11                    FREQuency:AUTO?
12                 In the “Command Descriptions,” the detailed descriptions of the individual commands are
13                 provided immediately after the command table, in the order in which the commands appear
                   in the table, reading from top to bottom.
14
15       5.2       Interpreting Syntax Flow Diagrams
                   Syntax flow diagrams are used extensively throughout the SCPI document and IEEE 488.2
16                 to provide pictorial representations of syntax. These representations are also known as
17                 railroad diagrams.

18                 The flow through a diagram is given by lines and arrows. These link together the various
                   objects used to form a command. Objects exist in the diagram as either a circle or a box.
19                 Circles indicate literal characters and the boxes represent a syntactic structure that is defined
20                 elsewhere in this document or in IEEE 488.2. Flow through the diagrams generally proceeds
                   left-to-right. Diagrams are entered on the left, and the syntax is satisfied when the diagram
21                 is exited on the right. When an element or group of elements in the diagram is repeatable, a
22                 reverse, right-to-left path will be shown around and above the element(s), and is marked with
                   a left-facing arrow. When an element or group of elements in the diagram are optional, a
23                 left-to-right bypass path will be shown around and below the element(s). A branch in the
24                 path indicates a choice of elements.

25                 Lowercase and uppercase letters are considered equivalent; however, no attempt has been
                   made to specify both alternatives in every instance. Whitespace characters (as defined in
26                 IEEE 488.2, section 7.4.1.2) are optional in many places, and no attempt has been made to
                   specify “optional whitespace” everywhere it may exist.

6       Program Headers
        Program headers are keywords that identify the command. The program headers follow the
        syntax described in section 7.6 of IEEE 488.2. Instruments shall accept both upper and
        lowercase characters without distinguishing between the cases. Program headers consist of
        two distinct types, common command headers and instrument-control headers.                          1
                                                                                                            2

        with the IEEE 488.2-defined common commands and queries. Their syntax is:                           4

6.2     Instrument-Control Headers
        Instrument-control headers are used for all other instrument commands, typically those             10
        related to source and measurement control. The syntax for instrument-control headers is:           11
                                                                                                           12
                                                                                                           13
                                                                                                           14
