                                                                                                           16
                                                                                                           17
        The definition of the effect of the colons in an instrument-control header is covered later in
        “Traversal of the Header Tree.”                                                                    18
6.2.1   Mnemonic Generation Rules                                                                          19
        Each instrument-control header or keyword has both a long and a short form. A SCPI                 20
        instrument shall accept only the exact short and the exact long forms. Sending a header that
        is not the short form, nor the complete long form to a SCPI instrument shall cause it to           21
        generate an error. IEEE 488.2 limits the length of a header to 12 characters, including any        22
        numeric suffix that may appear. The long form header is either a single word or an
        abbreviation of a phrase. The short form header is an abbreviation of the long form header.        23
        In order to maintain a consistent set of mnemonics, SCPI defines the rules to generate a           24
        mnemonic.
                                                                                                           25
        The long form mnemonic is generated from either a single word or a phrase. If a single word
        is used, then that word becomes the mnemonic. If a phrase is used, then the mnemonic is the        26


                                                                              Program Headers        6-1
                                               1999 SCPI Syntax & Style

                    first letter of each word and the entire last word. For example the phrase “relative velocity”
                    would generate RVELOCITY as the long form command header.
                    The short form mnemonic is usually the first four characters of the long form command
                    header. The exception to this is when the long form consists of more than four characters and
 1                  the fourth character is a vowel. In such cases, the vowel is dropped and the short form
                    becomes the first three characters of the long form. For example, the short form of FREE is
 2                  FREE, however, the short form of SWEEP is SWE. Note that elsewhere in this document a
 3                  special notation is employed to differentiate the short form keyword from the longform of
                    the same keyword. The long form of the keyword is shown, with the short form portion
 4                  shown in uppercase characters, and the rest of the keyword is shown in lowercase characters.
 5                  Thus Relative VELocity keyword would be shown as RVELocity.
     6              The short form generation rules imply that phrases such as “Jump Start” and “Jump Stop”
                    are not allowed. Although the long forms JSTART and JSTOP are unique, the short form is
 7                  the same in both cases, “JST.” This can be overcome by changing the phrases to “Jump
 8                  Begin” and “Jump End”, thus creating unique long and short forms. Alternatively, the
                    mnemonic JUMP can become an additional level in the tree, allowing STARt and STOP to
 9                  become their own mnemonics, giving JUMP:STARt and JUMP:STOP.
10                  The mnemonic generation rules allow keywords such as “TIME” and “TIMer” at the same
11                  tree level, since these are unique in both forms. This is not recommended since an unfamiliar
                    user may select the wrong function unintentionally. If the two functions have the same
12                  number and type of parameters, the instrument may not signal an error, further exacerbating
13                  the situation.
14                  All instrument command headers are allowed a numeric suffix to differentiate multiple
                    instances of the same structure, such as multi-channel instruments. The numeric suffix is
15                  applied to both the long and short forms. For example, TRIG1 is the short form of
16                  TRIGger1. A numeric suffix of 1 is implied on all instrument command headers that do not
                    explicitly define a suffix; thus, TRIG is equivalent to TRIG1.
17
                    As a general rule, a mnemonic should contain no digits. Ending a short or long form              1996
18                  mnemonic in a digit creates an ambiguity in separating the mnemonic from any added
19                  numeric suffix.
20       6.2.2      Building the Command Tree
                    SCPI commands are based on a hierarchical structure. This allows the same
21                  instrument-control header (keyword) to be used several times for different purposes,
22                  providing that the mnemonic occurs in a unique position in the hierarchy. That is, the
                    mnemonic does not collide with any other mnemonics at the same level, or one level
23
                    different where a default node exists.
24
                    Using hierarchical commands should eliminate the need for most multiword mnemonics.
25                  The use of multiword mnemonics is discouraged and they should only be used when:
26                      A).    The use of the hierarchical scheme would add several additional layers to the tree,
                               and


         6-2     Program Headers
                            1999 SCPI Syntax & Style

    B).    No further growth at the level of those potentially intermediate nodes is
           anticipated.
These style guidelines should act as a starting point for creating new commands.
1. The lowest nodes should have the broadest base possible. For example, the center
frequency command should be FREQuency:CENTer rather than CENTer:FREQuency. Since
                                                                                                        1
center is an adjective to the noun frequency, the tree will build with fewer duplicate nodes if         2
FREQuency:CENTer is chosen.
                                                                                                        3
2. If a function is broad-based and thought of as a separate subsystem, make it a separate
subsystem even if it could properly be classified under another subsystem. For example,
                                                                                                        4
bandwidth is a separate subsystem, even though it could be classified under frequency.                  5
Bandwidth is generally thought of as a separate subsystem and not classified with other
frequency commands by customers.
                                                                                                        6
3. Keep the tree as shallow as possible, usually three levels or less. If the tree for a given
                                                                                                        7
implementation is considerably deeper than it is wide, something may be wrong with the                  8
command structure.
                                                                                                        9
4. Some nodes may be made optional. When choosing to define a node as the default at a
particular level, be sure that it is the most common choice at that level. Also, check carefully
                                                                                                       10
for conflicting keywords, since all nodes below a default are effectively promoted by one              11
level when the default node is assumed.
                                                                                                       12
5. Some root keywords are optional, depending on the instrument capabilities. In an
instrument which is primarily a source, the root mnemonic [SOURce] is optional. [SENSe]
                                                                                                       13
is optional for instruments which are primarily sensors, and [ROUTe] is optional for                   14
scanners. This is at the discretion of the device designer. For horizontal compatibility
purposes, the instrument should accept this node if it is sent as part of a program message.
                                                                                                       15
6. A complete tree path shall be unique within SCPI. Thus, if a path is assigned a particular
                                                                                                       16
function in any instrument, it must perform the same function in all instruments which                 17
implement that path.
                                                                                                       18
7. SCPI also discourages the use of different keywords performing the same function. This
                                                                                                       19
problem is more difficult because of industry-standard terminology. A good example is
setting the output level on a source. Microwave sources call this power level, RF sources use          20
amplitude level, and power supplies use voltage level, yet the function is the same in all
                                                                                                       21
three. One of the tools available is to provide aliases for the function in order to provide both
sets of terminology. Whenever possible, SCPI shall implement as aliases those instances                22
where duplicate names are necessary. Where aliases are used, one term shall be defined
                                                                                                       23
which is the primary keyword. This keyword shall appear in all instruments.
                                                                                                       24
8. The tree structure shall follow the general form of the instrument model described in the
“Command Reference.”                                                                                   25
9. Implementations shall use the language constructs described in the “Command                         26
Reference,” if a construct exists for the desired feature. If the feature does not exist, the


                                                                        Program Headers          6-3
                                             1999 SCPI Syntax & Style

                  designer is responsible for following the life cycle described in an earlier chapter in order to
                  integrate the capability into SCPI.
                  10. The value or syntax of a parameter shall not change the type or number of other
                  parameters in that command. If such a condition is encountered, additional nodes should be
 1                added to the tree.
 2                For example, SCPI shall not include the structures such as:
                       :SYSTem
 3                       :BEEPer        1,<frequency>
 4                       :BEEPer        2,<time>
 5                Rather, SCPI uses a structure such as:
     6                :SYSTem
                         :BEEPer
 7                         :FREQuency <numeric_value>
 8                         :TIME         <numeric_value>
 9                11. In general, parameters should only appear at the leaf nodes of the tree. In the undesirable
10                example below, the command to set a single frequency is placed at a different level to the
                  commands that are used for setting a range (span) of frequencies. Conceptually equivalent
11                level commands are being placed at different levels, leading to possible misconceptions in
12                use. “Optional” nodes should be created as required to accomplish the same task. For
                  example, suppose an instrument superficially wants the following set of commands:
13                     FREQuency         <numeric_value>
14                       :CENTer         <numeric_value>
                         :SPAN           <Boolean>
15
16                The SCPI implementation shall overcome this by creating a node under frequency that
                  represents a command to set a single frequency, such as CW (Continuous Wave). Causing all
17                the command parameters to be associated with leaf nodes. To retain simple operation as in
18                the case of setting a single frequency, the CW node can be made optional, providing it does
                  not create a keyword conflict. Thus our example becomes:
19
                       FREQuency
20                       [:CW]             <numeric_value>
                          :CENTer          <numeric_value>
21
                          :SPAN            <Boolean>
22
                  Exceptions to this guideline are the AUTO and STEP constructs defined in this document.
23
                  The AUTO and STEP commands are formed from the leaf node for the value. Other
24                exceptions may be defined. In these cases, the exception shall be noted in the command
                  structure of the language document.
25
                  Nodes should not be added to a command tree simply to make the tree have a uniform depth.
26
                  If the only usable names for a terminal seem not to have any meaning (for instance, VALue),
                  the addition may not be helpful and the tree should be implemented unbalanced. An example

         6-4   Program Headers
                           1999 SCPI Syntax & Style

of this is the SOURce:FREQuency:SPAN node, which has the commands HOLD, LINK,
and FULL beneath it.
12. If a particular device function is not alterable or does not exist, then the associated SCPI
command need not be implemented unless the value of the function is different than the
defined *RST value for that function. If the *RST value is device-dependent, then the               1
function need not be implemented. For example:
                                                                                                    2
    A.      A source that has no amplitude modulation does NOT have to implement
            AM:STATe OFF because AM:STATe OFF is specified at *RST.
                                                                                                    3
    B.      A device that only sweeps in frequency (and has no CW function) must
                                                                                                    4
            implement FREQ:MODE SWEep because FREQ:MODE is specified as CW at                       5
            *RST. However, it is permissable to allow only SWEep as a parameter to
            FREQ:MODE.
                                                                                                    6
    C.      A device that produces a single, nonalterable CW frequency of 100 MHZ need
                                                                                                    7
            not accept FREQ[:CW] 100 MHZ since the *RST value of FREQ:CW is                         8
            device-dependent.
                                                                                                    9
The intent of this rule is to allow common features with varying complexities to be accessed.
This rule specifies the minimum conditions of including a node. However, designers are
                                                                                                   10
encouraged to include additional degenerate nodes which are important to their market. In          11
example A above, a designer may include AM:STATe OFF as a command, and is
encouraged to do so if the instrument is being targeted into markets where AM modulation is
                                                                                                   12
a typical feature of instruments in this market.                                                   13
13. A new command may not be added if there is already a command to control the same               14   FL005




functionality. This rule insures two instruments will not be needlessly incompatible when
designers choose arbitrarily among multiple commands available to control a particular
                                                                                                   15
function. (Notice that SCPI assures compatibility when aliased commands are implemented            16
by making one path required). A new command may not be added to the standard unless it
can be shown to control functions not controlled by any existing commands. The following
                                                                                                   17
guidelines may help in determining whether a command controls new functionality or                 18
represents illegal duplication, and guide selection of one command over another.
                                                                                                   19
         Does the setting of the new command affect the measurement result returned?
                                                                                                   20
Signal preconditioning commands (like ATTenuator, FILTer, GAIN) appear in the INPut
                                                                                                   21
subsystem and in SENSe. These commands are not aliases; The setting of
INPut:ATTenuator changes the reported signal level, while SENSe:ATTenuator would be                22
compensated for so the reported signal level would not be affected. Since these commands
                                                                                                   23
affect the returned value differently, they control different functions and are not duplicate
controls.                                                                                          24
         Does the new command control a function with a different purpose than any existing        25
         command?
                                                                                                   26
Numerical post-processing commands (like WINDow, AVERage, SMOothing) appear in the
sensor and also in CALC. The function properly belongs in the sensor when its purpose is to

                                                                      Program Headers        6-5
                                              1999 SCPI Syntax & Style

                    enhance accuracy or correct for artifacts introduced by the sensor. The function belongs in
                    CALCulate when its purpose is to change the presentation of the data or provide analytical
                    tools not directly related to measurement.
                           Does the command control measurement hardware?
 1                  Some functions (like SMOothing) may be performed directly on the signal in hardware or in
 2                  software after A/D conversion. While this rule can be difficult to apply, the fact that a
                    command controls measurement hardware often indicates that it belongs in the sensor rather
 3                  than CALCulate.
 4                         Does it make sense if the same operation may be done twice?
 5                  Another way to tell that a command controls new functionality is if it makes sense for the
     6              controlled function to appear twice in a single instrument. The AVERage subsystem is a
                    good example; it is not unreasonable to build an instrument that averages several readings to
 7                  improve the accuracy of the measurement, and also provides averaging as a statistical
 8                  function in the CALCulate subsystem.
 9                  14. In general, SCPI commands which are only events without a query form do not have any
                    parameters. Including a parameter might mislead a user into believing the value could be
10                  queried as most commands in SCPI have a query form, see 6.2.3.
                                                                                                                    HP082
11                  An exception to this guideline is when the action is performed on a named object within the
12                  instrument and these objects cannot be enumerated. For example, <file_name>,
                    <trace_name>, and <data_handle> are objects whose values cannot be entirely listed within
13                  SCPI. The user can create any number of <file_names> or <trace_names>. The signal
14                  routing concepts in SCPI allow a large number of possible <data_handles>.
                                                                                                                    HP082
15       6.2.3      Queries
16                  All commands, unless otherwise noted, have an additional query form. As defined in IEEE
                    488.2, a query is a command header with a question mark symbol appended (for example,
17                  FREQ:CENT?). When a query form of a command is received, the current setting associated
18                  with the command is placed in the output buffer. Query responses do not include the
                    command header. Execution of a query form has no side effects. It shall not cause any
19
                    settings or couplings within the instrument to change. An exception is in MEASurement
20                  subsystem, where instrument settings may change as a result of the measurement.
21                  Both the command and query forms shall be implemented unless a comment or note                  HP095
                    indicating otherwise appears in the keyword summary. Even when a command accepts only
22
                    a single selection, both the command and query forms shall still be implemented. A note of
23                  the form “[event; no query]” or “[no query]” indicates that only the command form and not
                    the query form shall be implemented. A note of the form “[query only]” indicates that only
24
                    the query form and not the command form shall be implemented.
25
                    When character data is used for a parameter, both longform and shortform values shall be
26                  recognized. If the command has a query form with character response data, the shortform
                    value is always returned.


         6-6     Program Headers
                                  1999 SCPI Syntax & Style

        When numeric parameters are queried, the result shall be returned in fundamental units
        unless otherwise specified or requested. When several different units may be considered
        fundamental (for example, dBuV or dBm), the units of the returned result shall be
        documented in the query response description for the command. A query may have a related
        :UNITs node to change the default units of the accepted or returned value, where this exists
        the coupling shall be clearly indicated in the command description.
                                                                                                           1
6.2.4   Traversal of the Header Tree
                                                                                                           2
        IEEE 488.2 allows the designer some discretion on how compound headers are handled                 3
        within the rules of section 7.6.1.5. SCPI imposes additional requirements regarding how a
        compound command is parsed.
                                                                                                           4
        Multiple <PROGRAM MESSAGE UNIT> elements may be sent in a <PROGRAM
                                                                                                           5
        MESSAGE>. The first command is always referenced to the root node. Subsequent                      6
        commands, however, are referenced to the same tree level as the previous command in a
        message unit. SCPI parsers shall follow the example presented in IEEE 488.2, section A.1.1.
                                                                                                           7
        A SCPI parser shall NOT implement the enhanced tree walking implementation described in            8
        section A.1.2.
                                                                                                           9
        For example, if a hypothetical instrument had the command tree:
             FREQuency
                                                                                                          10
               :STARt          <numeric_value>                                                            11
               :STOP           <numeric_value>
               :SLEW           <numeric_value>
                                                                                                          12
                 :AUTO         <Boolean> | ONCE                                                           13
               :BANDwidth <numeric_value>
             POWer
                                                                                                          14
               :STARt          <numeric_value>                                                            15
               :STOP           <numeric_value>
             BAND              A|B|C|D
                                                                                                          16
                                                                                                          17
        Then the following commands shall behave as described:
                                                                                                          18
                  FREQ:STAR 3 MHZ;STOP 5 MHZ<nl> shall set the start frequency to 3 MHz
                  and the stop frequency to 5 MHz.
                                                                                                          19
                  FREQ:STAR 3 MHZ;:FREQ:STOP 5 MHZ<nl> shall set the start frequency to 3
                                                                                                          20
                  MHz and the stop frequency to 5 MHz.                                                    21
                  FREQ:STAR 3 MHZ;POW:STOP 5 DBM<nl> may set the start frequency to 3                     22
                  MHz and shall generate an error because POW is not a node at the current parser
                  level.
                                                                                                          23
                  FREQ:STAR 3 MHZ;SLEW:AUTO ON<nl> shall set the start frequency to 3                     24
                  MHZ and couple the frequency slew rate.                                                 25
                  FREQ:SLEW:AUTO ON;STOP 5 MHZ<nl> may couple the slew rate and shall                     26
                  generate a command error since the coupling command is not at the same level as
                  the stop command.

                                                                           Program Headers          6-7
                                               1999 SCPI Syntax & Style

                               FREQ:SLEW 3 MHZ/S;AUTO ON<nl> may set the frequency slew rate to 3
                               MHZ/S and shall generate a command error because :AUTO is not at the same
                               level.
                               FREQ:START 3 MHZ;BAND 1 MHZ<nl> shall set the start frequency to 3 MHz
 1                             and the bandwidth to 1 MHz.
 2                             FREQ:START 3 MHz;:BAND A<nl> shall set the start frequency to 3 MHz and
                               select band A.
 3
                               FREQ:SLEW:AUTO ON;3 MHZ/S<nl> may couple the frequency slew rate and
 4                             shall generate a syntax error, because IEEE 488.2 specifies that headers must be
 5                             sent with each command.
     6              Default nodes in the tree shall not alter the header path of the parser in order to follow the
                    IEEE 488.2 rules for compound headers. IEEE 488.2, section 7.6.1.5 makes no mention of
 7                  default nodes, so adding something to the header path is not allowed. For example, if a
 8                  hypothetical instrument had the command tree:
                        DISPlay
 9                        [:STATe]          <Boolean>
10                         :DATA            <string>
11                  Then the following situations would have these results:
12                             DISP:STAT ON;DATA “Hello, world!”<nl> shall turn the display on and display
13                             “Hello, world!”.
14                             DISP ON;DATA “Hello, world!”<nl> may turn the display on and shall flag an
                               error (assuming that DATA is not a root mnemonic).
15
         6.2.5      Multiple Capabilities and Numeric Keyword Suffixes
16                  Many instruments provide multiple capabilities, by duplicating internal functional blocks.
17                  One example is an instrument that can display more than one measurement at a time.
                    Another example is an instrument that can make a particular measurement on one of several
18                  input channels. SCPI provides a mechanism to address this duplicate functionality while
19                  retaining the same hierarchy for each duplication.

20       6.2.5.1       Single Instrument with Many Electrical Ports
                    When only electrical ports (front panel terminals) are involved, the <channel_list> notation
21                  is sufficient to describe the measurement connection. An instrument which needs to select
22                  one or more of several input terminals can be logically modeled as a simple instrument with
                    one set of inputs connected to a scanner (signal multiplexor).
23
         6.2.5.2       Multiple Identical Capabilities
24                  When an instrument has several independent measurement channels (or other capabilities,
25                  such as displays or sources), the selection of which to use is designated by a numeric suffix
                    attached to a program mnemonic. If the suffix is absent, the command is treated as being
26                  designated for capability number one. In this way, channel one of a multiple channel
                    instrument can accept the same commands as a single channel instrument to allow for


         6-8     Program Headers
                                    1999 SCPI Syntax & Style

          upward compatibility. Further, adding multiple channels or capabilities to an instrument
          class where multiple channels were not anticipated becomes possible.
          The node that contains the numeric suffix is the one where the multiple capability occurs.
          This may be at any level of the tree: root, intermediate or terminal node. As an example,
          OUTP5:MOD3:FM2 would specify the second FM signal component of the third                            1
          modulation signal on the fifth output channel.
                                                                                                              2
          Devices which implement multiple channels/capabilities shall recognize nodes which do not
          have numeric suffixes and treat them as channel/capability 1. Instruments with a single
                                                                                                              3
          channel/capability are not required to accept a numeric suffix. This allows for upward              4
          compatibility.
                                                                                                              5
6.2.5.3      Logical Instruments
          A complex instrument such as a VXI card cage can be logically modeled as separate
                                                                                                              6
          instruments, each with its own (secondary) bus address. For example, common functions for           7
          all instruments can be located at secondary address 00, and otherwise each instrument
          responds individually to IEEE 488.2 commands. This requires that each logical instrument
                                                                                                              8
          (card) implement its own status model and I/O buffers.                                              9

         6-10   Program Headers

7       Parameters
          SCPI uses the parameter forms described in IEEE 488.2, section 7.7, with some additional
          restrictions. Also note that SCPI specifies the values for all commands upon receipt of
          *RST. In some cases, these reset values are device-dependent, but all measurement
          parameters must be set to some deterministic value for that particular instrument, which in          1
          turn must be documented in the instrument manual.                                                    2
7.1       Character Program Data                                                                               3
          Where possible, the same truncation rules are used for parameters as for headers. However,
          in many cases industry standards take precedence. For example, IDC is a better choice for            4
          DC current than anything SCPI rules would define, simply because it is an existing standard          5
          with wide acceptance. In addition, several character program data forms are predefined as
          extensions of <DECIMAL NUMERIC PROGRAM DATA>.                                                        6
7.2       Decimal Numeric Program Data                                                                         7
          Numeric elements shall be used only for representing numeric quantities. They shall not be           8
          used for selecting functions on a “One of N” position switch.
                                                                                                               9
          Implementations shall accept numeric data as described in IEEE 488.2, section 7.7.2.4.
          However, any number which exceeds +-9.9 E 37 shall generate an execution error (-222,               10
          “Data out of range”). Numbers shall be rounded to the closest “correct” value that the              11
          instrument accepts without error. This document does not define the value a parameter is set
          to if an out-of-range value is received.                                                            12
7.2.1     <numeric_value> Definition                                                                          13
          The decimal numeric element is abbreviated as <numeric_value> throughout this document.             14
          This is different from the <NRf> described in section 7.7.2.1 of IEEE 488.2 in several ways.
                                                                                                              15
          Several forms of <CHARACTER PROGRAM DATA> are defined as special forms of
          numbers. These are: MINimum, MAXimum, DEFault, UP, DOWN, Not A Number (NAN),                        16
          INFinity, and Negative INFinity (NINF). Individual commands are required to accept MIN              17
          and MAX. DEFault, UP, DOWN, NAN, INFinity, and NINFinity may be implemented at the
          discretion of the designer, in which case it shall be noted in the instrument documentation.        18
          Where an optional form is accepted, it will be noted in the command description.                    19
          A <non-decimal numeric> (IEEE 488.2, section 7.7.4), a <numeric_expression>, or a                   20
          <label> is part of <numeric_value> if an instrument implements these features.
                                                                                                              21
7.2.1.1   DEFault
          The special <numeric_value> parameter DEFault may be provided to allow the instrument to            22
          select a value for a parameter. When DEFault is sent, the instrument shall select a value           23
          which is deemed to be convenient to the customer. The setting may be device-dependent, or
          it may be defined as part of this standard. The use of DEFault is optional on a                     24
          command-by-command basis. Individual commands shall document where DEFault is                       25
          required.
                                                                                                              26
          For example, to use the SYST:TIME command to set a device’s clock ahead one hour
          (Daylight Savings Time), a program might send SYST:TIME UP,DEF,DEF<nl>.

                                                                                     Parameters         7-1
                                             1999 SCPI Syntax & Style

                   Another example is found in the MEASure commands. The syntax of the command which
                   measures DC voltage is:
                      MEASure:VOLTage:DC [<expected value>[,<resolution>]]
                   The MEASure command specifies that parameters are defaulted from the right and that any
 1                 parameter may be defaulted by using DEFault in place of the parameter. The following
 2                 command would measure DC voltage, defaulting the range to an instrument dependent value
                   (possibly autorange), but specifying the resolution at 0.001 Volt:
 3
                      MEASure:VOLTage:DC DEFault,0.001V
 4
         7.2.1.2   MINimum|MAXimum
 5                 The special form numeric parameters MINimum and MAXimum shall be provided which
 6                 assume the limit values for the parameter. The maximum and minimum shall be queryable
                   by sending <header>? MAXimum|MINimum. The MAXimum value refers to the largest
     7             value that the function can currently be set to, and MINimum refers to the value closest to
 8                 negative infinity that the function can be currently set to.
 9                 Some commands have multiple parameters. The query form of these commands returns a list
                   of values representing the current value of each of the parameters, in the order of their
10                 normal occurrence in a program message. If a MINimum/MAXimum query of multiple
11                 parameters is allowed, the keywords MINimum and MAXimum must occur as many times in
                   the query as there are parameters. MINimum requests that the instrument return the legal
12                 value which is closest to negative infinity for the parameter; MAXimum requests the legal
13                 value which is closest to positive infinity.
14                 For example, suppose an instrument implements the SYST:TIME command, which requires
                   three parameters, and allows MIN/MAX queries on this command. The following queries
15                 shall have these results:
16                           SYST:TIME?<nl> shall return the current setting of the time-of-day clock in the
17                           instrument.
18                           SYST:TIME? MAX,MAX,MAX<nl> could return 23,59,59.
19                           SYST:TIME? MAX<nl> shall set an error (-109, “Missing parameter”), since
                             three parameters are required and only one was sent.
20
         7.2.1.3   UP/DOWN
21                 An instrument may optionally allow the use of steps for some or all of its numeric entry. If
22                 steps are used, the keywords UP and DOWN shall be used as numeric parameters which
                   perform stepping. Steps may be adjustable through the step node for each individual
23                 parameter.
24                 The instrument may step a parameter when UP or DOWN is received in lieu of a numeric
25                 value. This capability is optional. However, if the capability is implemented, the device
                   shall include a node for each command which accepts step parameters. This node will
26                 specify the step. The step may either be a fixed linear size or a logarithmic number
                   representing number of decades/step.

         7-2   Parameters
                                      1999 SCPI Syntax & Style

7.2.1.3.1             STEP Subsystem Command Syntax
            The form of the step subsystem is as follows:
            :STEP
              [:INCRement]         <numeric_value>
               :PDECade            <numeric_value>                                                              1
               :MODE               LINear|LOGarithmic|L125|L13
               :AUTO               <Boolean>|ONCE
                                                                                                                2

                                                                                                                3
            This command controls the step size in absolute units when STEP:MODE LINear is selected.            4
            At *RST, this value is device-dependent.                                                            5
7.2.1.3.3             :PDECade <numeric_value>                                                                  6
            This command controls the number of steps per decade when STEP:MODE LOGarithmic is
            selected.
                                                                                                                7
            At *RST, this value is device-dependent.
                                                                                                                8

            meanings:
                                                                                                               11

                      the parameter.
                                                                                                               12

                      value of the function is x, the value of the function after executing an up shall be     14
                      determined by the following formula:

                                                                                                               19

                                                     

                      10

            Executing DOWN will set the value of the function to the next lower value in the sequence.         26

         7.2.1.3.6            STEP Subsystem Examples
 5                         FREQ:CENT:STEP 5 MHZ<nl>
 6                         FREQ:CENT UP<nl>
     7               sets the center frequency step to 5 MHz, and then increments the current value by 5 MHz.
 8                         BAND:RES 1MHZ<nl>
                           BAND:RES:STEP:MODE LOG;PDEC 3<nl>
 9                         BAND:RES UP<nl>
10                   The above sequence would specify a logarithmic step, set three steps/decade, and then
11                   increment the resolution bandwidth by 1/3 decade (logarithmic) to a final value of 2.154
                     MHz.
12
                           BAND:RES 1MHZ<nl>
13                         BAND:RES:STEP:MODE L125<nl>
14                         BAND:RES UP<nl>
15                   The above sequence would specify a 125 logarithmic sequence, and then increment the
                     resolution bandwidth to the next step in the sequence to a final value of 2.0 MHz.

         7.2.1.4     INFinity and Negative INFinity (NINF)
17                   A special case is made for infinity. Positive infinity is represented as 9.9 E 37. Negative
18                   infinity is -9.9 E 37. Instruments shall accept numbers within this range as valid numeric
                     data. They shall also limit response data to this range. If a valid instrument setting is infinity
19
                     or negative infinity, the values 9.9 E 37 and -9.9 E 37 shall be accepted and returned to
20                   represent positive and negative infinity respectively, and on input, the implementation shall
                     accept INFinity as an alias for positive infinity, and NINFinity as an alias for negative
21
                     infinity.
22
                     The numeric values for positive and negative infinity were chosen so that they fit into a
23                   32-bit IEEE 754 floating point number. This allows easy implementation using standard
                     tools in all popular languages and operating systems. Note that this does not limit the
24
                     numeric resolution. These values are larger than any quantities used or anticipated in
25                   instruments.
26       7.2.1.5     Not A Number (NAN)
                     Not a number is represented as 9.91 E 37. Not a number is defined in IEEE 754. Typical
                     applications are dividing zero by zero or subtracting infinity from infinity. Not a number is

         7-4   Parameters
                                   1999 SCPI Syntax & Style

        also used to represent missing data. A typical application is when a portion of a trace has not
        been acquired yet. On input, devices shall accept NAN as an alias for not a number.
        The numeric value for NAN was chosen so that it can be represented as a 32-bit IEEE 754
        floating point number. This allows easy implementation using standard tools in all popular
        languages and operating systems. Note that this does not limit the numeric resolution. This          1
        value is larger than any quantities used or anticipated in instruments.
                                                                                                             2
7.2.2   Unit Suffixes
        The <DECIMAL NUMERIC PROGRAM DATA> may be followed by an optional suffix.
                                                                                                             3
        All parameters which have associated units shall accept a suffix. Only suffixes appropriate          4
        for the command should be accepted. All suffixes must include the associated unit. See
        IEEE 488.2, 7.7.3, <SUFFIX PROGRAM DATA>, for a complete discussion of this topic.
                                                                                                             5
        Suffixes must accept multipliers except in cases where the multiplier is illogical, such as
                                                                                                             6
        dBm or PCT. Table 7-2 in IEEE 488.2 lists the allowed multipliers. If any of the multipliers         7
        are allowed with a suffix, then all the multipliers shall be interpreted properly. Compound
        suffixes are allowed.
                                                                                                             8
        If a suffix is included, the suffix and associated multiplier, if implemented, are applied to the
                                                                                                             9
        parameter. If the suffix is omitted, default units are used. The default unit is determined         10
        either from the :UNIT subsystem as described in 7.5 of Syntax & Style and in Chapter 23 of
        the Command Reference, or it is the fundamental unit associated with the parameter.
                                                                                                            11
        Fundamental units are either described in the appropriate subsystem or in the one shown in          12
        IEEE 488.2, table 7-1.
                                                                                                            13
7.3     Boolean Program Data
        The form <Boolean> is used throughout this document as a shorthand for the form
                                                                                                            14
        ON|OFF|<NRf>. Boolean parameters have a value of 0 or 1 and are unitless.                           15
        On input, an <NRf> is rounded to an integer. A nonzero result is interpreted as 1. This             16
        algorithm is the same as the one described in IEEE 488.2, section 10.25.3.
                                                                                                            17
        The <CHARACTER PROGRAM DATA> elements ON and OFF shall be accepted on input
        for increased readability. ON corresponds to 1 and OFF corresponds to 0.
                                                                                                            18
        Queries shall return 1 or 0, never ON or OFF.
                                                                                                            19
7.4     Coupling of Functions
                                                                                                            20
        There are two forms of coupling: functional and value. A coupling occurs when sending a             21
        command changes the value associated with another command. In general, functional
                                                                                                            22
        couplings are discouraged except in the MEASure subsystem. Value couplings are allowed
        if the coupling equations are well specified.                                                       23
        Some functions may have the ability to be decoupled. If functions can be decoupled, the             24
        ability to recouple them shall also exist. If a function cannot be decoupled, then a node to set
                                                                                                            25
        its value shall not exist, or shall be implemented as query-only. If a node is settable under
        some conditions, then the node may exist.                                                           26


                                                                                      Parameters      7-5
                                              1999 SCPI Syntax & Style

                    Another level in the tree is used to control coupling. The keyword AUTO shall be used to
                    control coupling. For example, the command to couple resolution bandwidth would be:
                          BAND:RES:AUTO ON
                    Setting a value explicitly for a function shall cause the function to be decoupled (:AUTO
 1                  OFF), if decoupling is possible. Otherwise an error shall be generated.
 2                  Selecting :AUTO ONCE shall cause the function to select the most appropriate value for
 3                  current conditions (range, signal level, etc), and then be decoupled. A subsequent query of
                    an :AUTO? will always return 0, since ONCE is an event which leaves the function in
 4                  AUTO OFF mode.
 5       7.4.1      Functional Coupling
 6                  Functional coupling occurs when a command causes side effects in the basic operating
                    mode of the device. An example is a command which sets the start frequency and also starts
     7              a sweep.
 8                  If a command which invokes a functional coupling is necessary, the instrument shall also
 9                  implement primitive commands which do not have functional couplings. The instrument
                    may then implement a complex command which is described as a combination of these
10                  primitive commands. This complex command may contain functional couplings, and must
11                  document the sequence of primitive commands used in its programming documentation.
12                  For example, if a source needs a command which sets the AM modulation level, and which
                    has the side effect of turning the modulation ON, the following could be implemented:
13
                    Primitives:
14                  AM
15                    :STATE               <Boolean>
                      [:DEPTh]             <numeric_value>
16
17                  Complex command added:
                    AM
18                    :SDEPth          <numeric_value>
19
                    Where AM:SDEPth is defined in the manual as:
20                  AM
21                  :DEPth             <numeric_value>;
                      :STATe           ON
22
         7.4.2      Value Coupling
23
                    The other form of coupling is called value coupling, which is allowed in SCPI. Values are
24                  coupled when a command changes the value of other numeric settings in the instrument. The
                    coupling relation would follow device-dependent equations. For example, bandwidth in a
25
                    receiver may be coupled to the frequency span. The individual command descriptions define
26                  these coupling equations.



         7-6     Parameters
                                   1999 SCPI Syntax & Style

        Groups of functions may be coupled in complex ways which affect the values for each other.
        For example START, STOP, CENTER, and SPAN are all value-coupled. CENTER is the
        arithmetic average of START and STOP. SPAN is the difference between START and
        STOP. Changing any one affects the value of two others.
7.4.3   Automatic Coupling                                                                                    1
        A special type of coupling is the automatic coupling. This is when the device provides an
        algorithm to select the value of a parameter. This algorithm could be based upon physical
                                                                                                              2
        inputs or other settings. When it is desirable to turn this algorithm on and off, the keyword         3
        AUTO is added. The AUTO command may accept parameters of ON|OFF|ONCE. ON
        enables the instrument algorithm. OFF disables the instrument algorithm. ONCE causes the
                                                                                                              4
        algorithm to be employed once, changing the associated parameter, and then reverting to               5
        AUTO OFF.
                                                                                                              6
7.5     Units of Measure and Suffixes
        Most of the information on units and suffixes is specified in IEEE 488.2, section 7.7.3.
                                                                                                              7
        However, further clarification is needed for units of power and amplitude, and for unitless           8
        quantities.
                                                                                                              9
7.5.1   Units of Amplitude and Power
                                                                                                             10
                   The fundamental unit of linear power is the Watt (W).
                                                                                                             11
                   The fundamental unit of linear amplitude is the Volt (V).
                                                                                                             12
                   The fundamental unit of logarithmic power is the dBm.
                                                                                                             13
                   The fundamental unit of logarithmic amplitude is the dBV.
                                                                                                             14
        Industry practices have caused other units to become widely used in various disciplines,
        particularly the units of uV, dBuV, dBuW and dBmV. Furthermore, many instruments cover               15
        a broad spectrum of applications where different units are considered the standard.                  16
        Therefore, instruments which implement commands whose parameters might be expressed in
        several different amplitude or power units shall provide the following means of setting and          17
        measuring amplitude and power functions:                                                             18
        If the unit is not specified, the default unit shall be that specified with a command in the         19
        UNIT subsystem, or a UNIT command in the appropriate sub-tree. The *RST values of
        settings in the UNIT subsystem shall be device-dependent. However, if a *RST unit is                 20
        different than the specified default unit, or is a logarithmic unit, then the command in the         21
        UNIT subsystem for that unit must be implemented.
                                                                                                             22
        If a suffix is sent with an <NRf>, the unit corresponding to that suffix shall override the
        default unit for that parameter.                                                                     23
        If an instrument accepts units from one of the classifications described above, it must accept       24
        all suffixes of that classification. For example, if an instrument accepts Watts, it must also       25
        accept uW, mW, etc. This includes all suffix multipliers described for that unit in IEEE
        488.2. However, it may, but is not required, to accept Volts as a unit. In instrument which          26
        accepts both requires a defined impedance for the conversion


                                                                                     Parameters        7-7
                                            1999 SCPI Syntax & Style


                             Voltage2
                  (Power=             )
                            Impedance


                  either explicitly through an input or output impedance command or implicitly if the
 1                impedance of the instrument is known and fixed. A further restriction, is that if an
 2                instrument accepts logarithmic units, it shall also accept the comparable linear unit. For
                  example, an instrument which accepts dBms must also accept Watts, MW, UW, etc. For
 3                example:
 4                   POW:UNIT DBUV<nl>
 5                   POW:LEV 50<nl>

 6                shall set the amplitude level to 50 dBuV.

     7               POW:UNIT DBM<nl>
                     POW:LEV 5V<nl>
 8
                  would set the power level to 5 Volts.
 9
                  Since some instruments are used in applications where both power and voltage units are
10                appropriate, the system’s impedance may be important to the user. This impedance is
11                needed to do the conversion between power and voltage (and maybe even current). All
                  instruments are encouraged to provide a node for at least querying this impedance. The node
12                shall be called :IMPedance, and will generally appear under the INPut or OUTPut
13                subsystem. Open circuits shall be expressed by setting IMPedance INFinity. It is therefore
                  possible to express output power in Volts:
14
                     POW:UNIT V<nl>
15                   OUTP:IMP 50 OHM<nl>POW:LEV 5<nl>
16                would set the power level to 5 Volts into a 50 Ohm load, or 0.5 Watt.
17                It is also sometimes necessary to determine which amplitude measurement is being made.
18                Therefore, a measurement qualification may be appended to the suffix. The suffix
                  appendices are described as:
19
                             PK: Peak amplitude
20
                             PP: Peak-to-peak amplitude
21
                             RMS: RMS amplitude
22
                  If no suffix appendix is specified, the default is device-dependent. However, all instruments
23                shall accept the suffix appendix for all types they support.
24                For example, a voltmeter which measures RMS voltage shall accept the suffixes V and
25                VRMS. A function generator which outputs peak voltage would accept the suffixes V and
                  VPK. An RF signal source might accept dBUV, dBUVRMS and dBUVPK.
26

7.5.2   Expressing Unitless Quantities
        The ratio of two linear quantities shall default to a unitless ratio (A/B). For example, if the
        input power for a system is 5 Watts, and the output power is 20 Watts, the power gain =
        20W/5W = 4.
        The difference between two logarithmic quantities shall be expressed in dB. For example if           1
        the input power of a system is 3 dBm and the output power is 5 dBm then the gain of the
        system is 5 dBm-3 dBm=2 dB.
                                                                                                             2
        Under exceptional conditions other units may be used for the ratio of two quantities. A valid
                                                                                                             3
        exception would be if a standards-setting organization (Bell, CCITT, military, IEEE, IEC,            4
        etc.) specifies that a measurement shall be made using a special unit like PCT (percent).
                                                                                                             5

8.1    Function
       The <EXPRESSION PROGRAM DATA> described in IEEE 488.2 is more tightly defined                        DIF01
                                                                                                          TWV41C
       in this section. SCPI defines five types of expressions, numeric expressions, channel lists,         1
       numeric lists, Data Interchange Format (dif) expressions, and instrument specifier
       expressions. The dif expressions are defined in Volume 3, “Data Interchange Format.”                 2
       Instrument specifiers are defined in Volume 4, “Instrument Class Applications.”                      3
       Other expression types may be added in future releases of this document, including but not           4
       limited to logical expressions, trigger expressions, and sequence expressions. Other uses of
       IEEE 488.2 expressions are legal, and may be documented in the individual command                    5
       descriptions.                                                                                        6
8.2    Usage                                                                                                7
       The use of expressions is optional in SCPI. For expression types defined in this section, it is      8DIF01

                                                                                                           22

8.3.1.2   Precedence Rules
                                                                                                              9
          Expressions shall be evaluated according to the following precedence rules:                        10
              1. Enclosed by parentheses
              2. Unary operators (+ and -)
                                                                                                             11
              3. ^(exponentiation)                                                                           12
              4. * (multiplication), / (division), MOD and DIV
              5. + (addition) and - (subtraction)
                                                                                                             13
              6. NOT                                                                                         14
              7. AND
              8. OR and EXOR
                                                                                                             15
              9. Left to right                                                                               16
8.3.1.3   Semantics                                                                                          17
          As stated in the syntax diagram, expressions may contain terms which are numbers, traces,
          variables, or expressions.
                                                                                                             18
          Elements in a numeric expression are promoted to the size and type of the most complex
                                                                                                             19
          element, and the result of the expression is of that type. That is, an expression containing a     20
          <trace_name> will be evaluated according to the rules for arithmetic on traces, and the result
          will be a trace. If an expression contains both a <trace_name> and scalar data, a trace is
                                                                                                             21
          created with all elements set to the value of the scalar data before arithmetic is performed.      22
          For example, if TREF is a trace_name, the expression (TREF-3) results in a trace the same
          size as TREF, with each data element lower by three.
                                                                                                             23
8.3.2     Channel Lists
                                                                                                             24
          Channel lists are used to specify electrical ports on an instrument. They are typically used for   25
          signal routing either in a standalone switch box or in an instrument with multiple input
                                                                                                             26
          channels. An instrument with multiple channels may or may not do any signal switching as


                                                                                      Expressions      8-3
                                            1999 SCPI Syntax & Style

                  the result of a channel list. Completely separate sensing channels are allowed, but may
                  appear to the language the same as channels which are switched.

 1                through 6. Whether the measurements are performed simultaneously or in the order in the
                  list is unspecified. Channel lists are also used by the ROUTe subsystem, “Command
 2                Reference,” 15.1.

through 3, but row 1, column 1 through 3 and next row 2 column 1 through 3. This method          17
provides a functional compatibility between commands sent to matrix switches with

9   Status Reporting
    SCPI requires the status mechanism described in chapter 11 of IEEE 488.2, including full
    implementation of the Event Status register structure.
    A SCPI device shall include the SCPI-defined OPERation status register and QUEStionable               1  Edchange




    data/signal status register with the associated condition, event, and enable commands. In
    Figure 9-1 on the following page, “Minimum Status Reporting Structure Required by SCPI”,              2
    a pictorial representation is given that shows the core of the SCPI-required status reporting         3
    capability. Additional requirements are established for instruments that support either
    multiple logical INSTruments or the expanded capability TRIGger model.                                4
    In general, a status register should fit into a 16-bit integer with the most-significant bit          5
                                                                                                         TK046
    always zero (positive logic).                                                                         6
    In the figures in this chapter, an elongated box is used to represent the “Status Data                7
    Structure-Register Model,” which is defined in IEEE 488.2. SCPI consists of condition,
    event, enable and optional transition registers. Two concentric circles with a cross through          8
    the center one indicates a logical summing.                                                           9

9.1   The Device-Dependent Register Model
      The Device-Dependent Register model follows the structure described in IEEE 488.2,
      section 11.4.2. The transition filter described in figure 11-6 is actually a pair of
      programmable transition filters which are described below.
      The commands which access these registers are described in the “SCPI Language                         1
      Description.”
                                                                                                            2
      If the Error/Event Queue Summary is reported in the Status Model, then bit 2 of the Status
      Byte shall be used to reflect the Empty/Non-Empty status of the queue. A bit value of 1               3
      indicates the queue is not empty. See the SYSTem:ERRor subsystem, Command Reference,                  4
      21.8.
                                                                                                            TK012
                                                                                                            5
9.2   Transition Filters                                                                                    6
      Transition filters are described in IEEE 488.2, section 11.4.2.2.1. SCPI allows the use of            7
      programmable transition filters. When transition filters are used, SCPI requires the use of
      separate positive and negative transition filters. A positive transition filter allows an event to    8
      be reported when a condition changes from false to true. A negative filter allows an event to         9
      be reported when a condition changes from true to false. Setting both positive and negative
      filters true allows an event to be reported anytime the condition changes. Clearing both             10
      filters disables event reporting.                                                                    11
      The contents of transition filters are unchanged by *CLS and *RST.                                   12
9.3   Operation Status Register                                                                            13
      The OPERation status register contains conditions which are part of the instrument’s normal
      operation.
                                                                                                           14
      The definition of each of these bits (condition register) is as follows:
                                                                                                           15
                 0-CALibrating — The instrument is currently performing a calibration.
                                                                                                           16
                 1-SETTling — The instrument is waiting for signals it controls to stabilize               17
                 enough to begin measurements.                                                             18
                 2-RANGing — The instrument is currently changing its range.                               19
                 3-SWEeping — A sweep is in progress.                                                      20
                 4-MEASuring — The instrument is actively measuring.                                       21
                 5-Waiting for TRIG — The instrument is in a “wait for trigger” state of the               22
                 trigger model.
                                                                                                           23
                 6-Waiting for ARM — The instrument is in a “wait for arm” state of the trigger
                 model.                                                                                    24
                 7-CORRecting — The instrument is currently performing a correction.                       25
                                                                                                           26

                              13-INSTrument Summary Bit One of n multiple logical instruments is

         9.4       QUEStionable Data/Signal Status Register
 4                 The QUEStionable status register set contains bits which give an indication of the quality of
 5                 various aspects of the signal.

 6                 A bit set in the condition register indicates that the data currently being acquired or
                   generated is of questionable quality due to some condition affecting the parameter associated
 7                 with that bit. For example, if the FREQ bit were set, this would mean that the frequency
 8                 accuracy of the signal was of questionable quality.

     9             The frequency bit might, in turn, have a register set associated with it, further refining the         EdChange




                   error into device-dependent conditions such as loop unlocked, oven cold, or reference signal
10                 missing. This layering of registers is called “fan-out”. See Figure 9-2 for an illustration of
11                 this technique. The device designer should be aware that adding registers to the status model
                   increases complexity. At the same time, it may be the only way to communicate time
12                 sensitive status information to the instrument controller.
13
14
15

22                 Figure 9-2 Hierarchical Expansion of the QUEStionable Status Register
23                 Bit 14 is defined as the Command Warning bit. This bit indicates a non-fatal warning that          TK048
                   relates to the instrument’s interpretation of a command, query, or one or more parameters of
24
                   a specific command or query. Setting this bit is a warning to the application that the resultant
25                 instrument state or action is probably what was expected but may deviate in some manner.
26


         9-4   Status Reporting
                                 1999 SCPI Syntax & Style

      For example, the Command Warning bit is set whenever a parameter in one of the                    TK048
      Measurement Instruction commands or queries is ignored during execution. Such a
      parameter may be ignored because it cannot be specified by a particular instrument.
      Bit 13, INSTrument summary, is described later in this chapter in association with multiple
      logical instruments.                                                                               1
      Bits in both OPERation and QUEStionable status registers may be redefined by the                   2
      application programmer. This optional feature allows an application program to configure
      two registers in whatever form it likes. Any error or event number from the entire pool of
                                                                                                         3
      errors/events the instrument can generate may be mapped into any bit of the OPERation or           4
      QUEStionable register.
                                                                                                         5
      For example, an application program controlling a voltmeter may choose to map VOLTage
      event X, VOLTage event Y and VOLTage event Z directly into the QUEStionable register
                                                                                                         6
      so that it has more direct access to them. Another purpose for this feature is to minimize the     7
      need for adding complex hierarchical registers to the status model. The mapping is
      controlled by the STATus:OPERation:MAP and STATus:QUEStionable:MAP commands.
